description: We are middle school students from TED Üsküdar College in Istanbul, Türkiye. We are interested in space, science, technology, and coding. We enjoy solving problems, creating new ideas, and working as a team. We are excited to learn and create together in the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
What would you need to live on Mars? Our team, TED Üsküdar Cosmic Coders, created Mars Mission Trainer, a Scratch game that helps children explore this question through ten connected training days.

Players travel to Mars, read a real terrain map, connect an energy system, calculate water recovery, compare food-growing times and prepare a base. They also answer questions about methane and learn why detecting it does not automatically prove that life exists.

We used NASA Mars Trek imagery, NASA information about water recovery and methane, and Canadian Space Agency educational resources. These sources become short activities in which players make choices, receive feedback and try again.

Our project responds to the “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge by turning space science into an interactive story. We want children to think about how water, energy, food and scientific evidence affect decisions. The game is a simplified learning experience, not a realistic mission simulation.
details:
MARS MISSION TRAINER
TED Üsküdar Cosmic Coders

OUR PURPOSE

What would we need to live on Mars? We created Mars Mission Trainer to help children explore this question through a Scratch game.

Our goal is to help players understand the importance of water, energy, food and protection, while learning to make decisions using scientific information. We also want players to question evidence: finding something interesting on Mars does not automatically prove that life exists there.

OUR SOLUTION

Our project responds to the “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge. It brings ten connected training days into one adventure, from travelling towards Mars to setting up a base.

Players complete short activities involving navigation, map reading, connecting equipment, answering questions and managing resources. Each task introduces a need that connects to the next part of the story.

The missions include:

• Guiding a spacecraft and avoiding obstacles.
• Reading a real Mars elevation map.
• Connecting a solar panel, controller, battery and water device.
• Calculating water recovery and water loss.
• Exploring basic needs and food production.
• Preparing protective equipment.
• Completing an observation and communication task.
• Investigating what methane can—and cannot—tell us about Mars.
• Exploring a wind-energy activity.
• Adding water storage and power equipment to a final base.

The game combines student-created drawings and Scratch activities with scientific reference material. It is an educational model, not a realistic astronaut simulator or an engineering design for a Mars settlement.

HOW WE USE SPACE AGENCY RESOURCES

Mars maps

The map-reading activity uses a static Mars elevation image associated with NASA Mars Trek and Mars Global Surveyor’s Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA). Players compare two marked locations and use the map colours to identify lower terrain.

The activity also explains that elevation alone cannot determine whether a landing or base location is safe.

Water recovery

The water activity uses NASA’s report of a 98% water-recovery milestone aboard the International Space Station. Players apply this percentage to simple quantities and calculate how much water is recovered or lost.

We use this as an example of why recycling matters in space. It is an ISS achievement, not a measurement from an operating Mars base.

Food production

Canadian Space Agency educational resources informed the food-production activity. Players compare crops and consider how growing time affects planning.

These are reference examples for learning about food production. They do not show that crops have already been grown on Mars.

Methane and scientific evidence

NASA’s Curiosity methane information and its explanation of possible methane sources and sinks informed our methane activity.

Players consider three important ideas: Curiosity has detected methane on Mars; methane can have biological and non-biological sources; and methane detection alone does not prove that life exists.

David A. Weintraub’s book, Life on Mars: What to Know Before We Go, was an additional reading source for our discussion of Mars and possible life.

WHAT PLAYERS CAN LEARN

By completing the missions, players can practise:

• Reading information from a scientific map.
• Applying percentages to water conservation.
• Understanding connections between energy and essential equipment.
• Considering food and resource needs.
• Distinguishing an observation from a conclusion.
• Learning from feedback and trying again.

We designed the game to encourage curiosity and discussion. We have not formally measured its effect on learning.

HOW TO PLAY

Open the shared Scratch project:


https://scratch.mit.edu/projects/1440505143

Click the green flag, then follow the instructions on the screen. Different missions use keyboard controls, mouse clicks, dragging or typed answers.

In the map activity, type 1 or 2 and press Enter. In the cable activity, connect the numbered cables and click TEST SYSTEM. In the methane activity, choose TRUE or FALSE and use the on-screen buttons to continue.

Click the green flag to restart the game.

TEAM CONTRIBUTIONS AND AI ASSISTANCE

Our team consists of five students from TED Üsküdar College. Students contributed game ideas, drawings and individual Scratch sections. Our teacher coordinated the work and supported the scientific explanations and preparation of the submission.

We used ChatGPT (OpenAI) to help develop and revise code, troubleshoot errors, combine separate Scratch sections, and improve some activities and story transitions. ChatGPT also supported English translation and editing, source research and organisation, and preparation of the presentation and project description.

The team logo was generated using ChatGPT and is labelled “AI-generated with ChatGPT”.

ChatGPT was used during development. The Scratch game itself does not contain a live chatbot or an AI model.
